title: State-Dependent Safety Failures in Multi-Turn Language Model Interaction
claim: A two-stage procedure initializes a benign conversational state, then evolves it step by step toward a boundary crossing, unlike static prior attacks.
layout: 2 columns: left stage I/II dialogue flow top-down, right latent-space plot
description: The figure has two parts. The left, in dashed boxes, shows the two-stage pipeline. Stage I (State Initialization) starts with a refused harmful prompt. It then shows a softened prompt, assigned roles, and a benign dialogue history with a structured turn template. Stage II (State Evolution) is a vertical chain of chat turns between cartoon robot icons. Orange boxes hold model replies with harmfulness scores J1 to J5. Green dashed boxes show history updates with retry generate and retry fallback interventions. The right, on a blue background, compares STAR with ActorAttack. It uses node chains for tree and linear trajectories and a 2-D latent-space plot with a dashed safety boundary and arrows from z0 to z1. A large arrow reads 'Deterministic State Evolution Toward Compliance'. A harmfulness color bar and the auxiliary and target models sit at the bottom.
caption: Overview of STAR. The framework operates in two stages: (1) state initialization via semantic-preserving softening, query-aware role generation, and structured turn template, and (2) state evolution via role-conditioned multi-turn interaction with feedback-aware history intervention and trajectory control.
abstract: Safety alignment in large language models is typically evaluated under isolated queries, yet real-world use is inherently multi-turn. Although multi-turn jailbreaks are empirically effective, the structure of conversational safety failure remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we study safety failures from a state-space perspective and show that many multi-turn safety failures in current safety-aligned language models arise from contextual state evolution, a regime that is not fully captured by isolated prompt-level analyses alone. We introduce STAR, a state-oriented diagnostic framework that treats dialogue history as a state transition operator and enables controlled analysis of safety behavior along interaction trajectories. Rather than optimizing attack strength, STAR provides a principled probe of how aligned models traverse the safety boundary under autoregressive conditioning. Across multiple frontier language models, we find that systems that appear robust under static evaluation can undergo rapid and reproducible safety collapse under structured multi-turn interaction. Mechanistic analysis reveals monotonic drift away from refusal-related representations and abrupt phase transitions induced by role-conditioned context. Together, these findings motivate viewing language model safety as a dynamic, state-dependent process defined over conversational trajectories.
